summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the surviving sodomy-law articles resolved that the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct; those articles had reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision for heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy. The outcome settles the criminal-law question but leaves the wider framework untouched: there is no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and no recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriage.

There is no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor has no route to have a chosen name or gender marker reflected in documents, and the Dominican authorities recognise no domestic process for it.

The Dominican Republic accepted recommendations at its Universal Periodic Review on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and on the rights of intersex persons. The review record shows the commitments being accepted without any accompanying detail on domestic implementation, so no statute, regulation or complaint mechanism follows from them in the sources available.

Documented violence against trans women in the Dominican Republic is high and falls hardest on the most marginalised, in particular trans sex workers. The country's longest-standing trans-led organisation, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers (COTRAVETD), co-founded in 2004, has recorded the community's conditions first-hand for two decades.

Tourist enclaves such as Punta Cana and Puerto Plata operate as insulated resort environments under international scrutiny, and Santo Domingo has a visible trans community and an annual Pride caravan. Beyond those settings, machista culture shapes daily life and police harassment of trans people is a documented feature of enforcement practice, so visibility carries risk that varies sharply by place and by who is present.
tangentialFactors:
Organised domestic opposition to LGBT visibility has been demonstrated at the highest levels of diplomatic contact. The June 2015 Santo Domingo appearance of the openly gay US ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster alongside his husband triggered a sustained backlash that included attacks on LGBT Dominicans, and his two-year tenure exposed a polarised climate. When he departed in early 2017, observers noted that his absence left an advocacy void; he had spoken at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016.

Counterweights exist. More than 300 activists from across Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT and intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo in April 2017, at which Dominican government officials spoke, and Brazilian authorities formally recommended anti-discrimination legislation to the Dominican Republic at the 2024 UPR. The pattern is one of official engagement coexisting with entrenched organised hostility rather than a consistent line from the state.

Regional comparisons: several neighbouring and peer Caribbean states retain criminal penalties for consensual same-sex conduct, which places the Dominican Republic's settled decriminalisation ahead of parts of its immediate neighbourhood while leaving it behind on protective legislation.
localsOnly:
COTRAVETD, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, was co-founded in 2004 and is directed by Nairovi Castillo, who has spoken publicly about trans conditions in the country on international observances such as the Transgender Day of Visibility. It remains a principal point of organisation for trans sex workers, who face the sharpest exposure to violence.

Residents have no statutory avenue to challenge discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, health care or public services, and no route to legal gender recognition. The accepted UPR recommendations on SOGI discrimination and intersex rights have not been converted into domestic law that a resident could invoke.

Santo Domingo supports an annual Pride caravan and a visible community infrastructure, and Dominican officials have appeared at regional LGBT conferences hosted in the capital. Access to that infrastructure is concentrated in the capital and does not extend to most of the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the source inventory for this pass contains nothing on entry or visa screening, on document or marker rules applied to travellers at the border, on hate-crime sentencing enhancements, or on access to gender-affirming care. Absence here means not sourced, not that the position is permissive.

The UPR record shows accepted recommendations on intersex rights and SOGI discrimination with no domestic implementation detail attached; whether any implementing measure has since been drafted is unresolved in these sources.

The material on the Brewster ambassadorship and the 2017 Santo Domingo conference is LGB-focused. It is used here only as evidence of the hostility and polarisation a trans visitor would be entering, not as direct documentation of trans-specific incidents.
